# Policy Atlas v3 Backend Architecture Briefing

Core message: Policy Atlas v3 is not a document generator. It is an AI-enabled policy analysis workspace for building an inspectable decision-support body: artefacts, evidence, provenance, comments, versions, dependencies and decision logs that humans use to brief, advise and write outside the tool.

How to use this briefing. This document gives the shared mental model for the Policy Atlas team. It compresses the full living backend architecture note into the product boundary, backend principles, architecture map, v3.0 execution model and build implications. The full architecture note remains the source for detailed status tags, unresolved questions and implementation-level decisions.

In this briefing:

* What the backend is for, and what v3.0 is deliberately not trying to solve.  
* The design principles that translate the v3 UX into backend architecture.  
* The seven-layer architecture and the core object model.  
* How a run works from user intent to inspectable, progressively-disclosed artefacts.  
* How provenance, trust, steering, collaboration and audit are handled.  
* The build-light execution posture and the seams left open for later.

# 1\. Executive summary

The backend exists to make AI-assisted policy analysis usable in high-pressure government work without sacrificing traceability. Users should experience a guided policy-analysis workspace; underneath, the backend supplies the evidence handling, orchestration, provenance, collaboration, versioning and audit machinery that make that workspace trustworthy.

The product boundary is central. A project is a policy workstream, not a single search or report. Its terminal product is a decision-support body: artefacts produced by capabilities, the corpus of evidence and extracted data behind them, significant-claim provenance, comments and challenges, versions, dependencies and the decision log. Humans then use this body to brief, advise, write, clear and publish outside Policy Atlas. The tool supports policy judgement; it does not replace it.

The architecture is artefact-centred and evidence-led. Chat is the orchestration surface, not the product. Artefacts are the visible unit of value; blocks are the unit of storage, versioning, commenting and regeneration; addressable units inside blocks anchor claims, citations, gaps, patterns, comments and later eval results. Evidence sits in a shared information layer and is reused across capabilities rather than trapped inside one run.

The central tension is agency versus accountability. Agents should have bounded freedom over method \- how to search, sequence, synthesise, compare and recover from thin evidence. Humans retain authority over substance \- options, recommendations, assumptions, counterfactuals, value judgements and material deviations from the plan. Steering modes change involvement frequency, not this authority boundary.

The v3.0 build posture is deliberately light. v3.0 uses serial orchestration, an off-request worker tier, LangGraph checkpoints on Postgres, a runs table, block-boundary commits, tool-result memoisation and a separate canonical Project event log (the single append-only spine; the decision log, change log, version history and catch-me-up are projections over it). Heavy durable workflow engines, branch-level parallelism, formal clearance, artefact-scoped permissions and per-item egress controls are deferred behind seams.

The test for v3.0: can a policy team start from intent, get an editable plan, run declared capabilities, inspect evidence and gaps, steer substance-shaping choices, collaborate around artefacts, read analysis at multiple levels of detail by drilling from summaries into full grounded detail, and understand what changed? Sharing and export of cited artefacts \- with version-pinned deep links back into the body \- are held as a deferred seam rather than a v3.0 build.

# 2\. Product and backend boundary

The backend is responsible for the tight evidence-and-scrutiny loop where Policy Atlas is distinctive. It manages projects, artefacts, blocks, versions, comments, users and decision logs; ingests and structures evidence; orchestrates capability sub-agents through human-readable plans; produces grounded artefact blocks; preserves the distinction between agent-proposed, user-steered and human-decided material, with human-authored and human-amended content representable in provenance when the deferred editing UX lands; and makes runs durable enough for human-in-the-loop use.

| In scope for v3.0 | Out of scope for v3.0 |
| :---- | :---- |
| Projects as policy workstreams; decision-support bodies as the product of the system. | Automatically writing the final government white paper or policing every claim lifted into external documents. |
| Evidence ingestion, retrieval, screening, appraisal, extraction and reuse through a shared information layer. | A general-purpose agent platform or a free-form tool palette for agents. |
| Declared capabilities that produce inspectable artefacts through bounded plans. | Full departmental clearance workflow, Teams/Word replacement or formal organisation-wide consensus engine. |
| Grounded blocks, structured provenance, evidence gaps, pattern annotations and source appraisal. | Full RBAC, artefact-scoped visibility and per-document sensitivity gates before any v3.0 behaviour reads them. |
| Anchored comments, catch-me-up, versioning, lock-on-advance and decision logs. | Private deployments for the most sensitive cases, though seams are preserved for later. |

The practical consequence: when in doubt, v3.0 should favour features that improve the inspectable body \- evidence, artefacts, provenance, comments, version history and audit \- over features that imply a broader workflow the tool does not yet drive.

# 3\. Backend design principles

The UX principles are: guide don't overwhelm, modular but coherent, designed for judgement, built for collaboration, and evidence-led and inspectable. The backend translates these into the principles below. They should be used to resolve product, data-model and execution questions during implementation.

| Principle | Implementation implication |
| :---- | :---- |
| Progressive complexity | Store rich structure, but reveal it when useful: plan before run, evidence behind claims, comments beside blocks, source appraisal when judging trust, blast radius when rerunning. |
| Artefacts over chat | Chat coordinates work. Artefacts and the evidence behind them are the work product; the project memory is a structured state, not a transcript. |
| Reusable evidence substrate | Evidence operations write reusable state to the information layer. Analysis capabilities read from that layer and produce artefacts. |
| Provenance generated with claims | Significant claims are emitted with citations, quotes, grounding tier and appraisal labels; citations are never attached after prose is written. |
| Bounded agent agency | Agents operate inside declared capability specs, component skeletons, scoped tools and escape hatches. |
| Humans decide substance | Agents may decide bounded method; humans gate policy options, recommendations, assumptions, counterfactuals, value judgements and material deviations. |
| Plan as audit spine | The human-readable plan is canonical and editable. Machine config is compiled from approved plan fields, not hidden in parallel. |
| Collaboration anchored to work | Comments attach to blocks, units, rows, cells, claims, gaps or sources, and the agent can act on them. |
| Build light, leave seams | Meet v3.0 needs without prematurely adopting infrastructure for deferred complexity. Preserve seams for parallelism, private deployment, richer security and workflow-engine substitution. |
| Model only what behaves |  Do not create labels, object types, or flags in the backend unless they actually change system behaviour in v3.0. |
| Decompose for eval | The tool \-\> component \-\> capability \-\> artefact \-\> project hierarchy is also the audit and evaluation surface. |

# 4\. Architecture at a glance

![][image1]

*Figure 1\. Simplified v3.0 backend flow: one user-facing orchestrator, declared capability sub-agents, shared information layer, grounded artefact blocks and structured annotations.*

| Layer | What it contains |
| :---- | :---- |
| Project and workspace | Workspaces, projects, artefacts, blocks, versions, the decision-support body and export/share seam metadata where explicitly scoped. |
| Information | Source snapshots, frozen parsed chunks as the content of record, retrieval passages and embeddings, extracted findings and coverage records, appraisals, structured columns, tags, artefacts and retrieval/scoping state. Original bytes are not retained. |
| Capability | Declared capabilities, component skeletons, capability sub-agents, tool scopes, dependencies and output shapes. |
| Planning and orchestration | Orchestrator/co-pilot, orchestration plans, per-capability commits, steering modes, check-ins and dependency graph. |
| Trust and provenance | Claims, citations, supporting quotes, evidence gaps, patterns, grounding tiers, appraisal labels, comments and eval annotations. |
| Collaboration and audit | Orchestrator thread, companion transcripts, private Q\&A, anchored comments, lock-on-advance, catch-me-up, version history and the canonical Project event log. |
| Execution and deployment | Off-request workers, serial v3.0 orchestration, LangGraph checkpointer, Postgres/Aurora, runs table, memoisation, own-AWS, and configured inference routes behind an in-house routing layer. |

# 5\. Core mental model and data model

![][image2]

*Figure 2\. Core object model: capabilities produce artefacts; artefacts contain blocks; blocks expose addressable units; annotations attach to units and can be queried across the project.*

The model to keep in mind is simple but strict. Tools are shared callable operations. Components are steps inside a capability. Capabilities are artefact-producing compositions of components, tools, dependencies and output shapes. Artefacts are the visible unit of value. Blocks are the unit of storage, versioning, interaction and regeneration. Addressable units inside blocks \- spans, rows, cells or stable sub-block units \- are what provenance, comments, gaps, patterns and eval scores attach to.

The shared information layer is the substrate across capabilities. It holds the corpus, the artefacts, source metadata, embeddings, retrieval state, extraction outputs, appraisal outputs, structured columns and tags. Organisation is handled through tags plus scoping: tags are item-level labels, while scoping is the behaviour of telling an agent where to look first. Scoping is a soft retrieval prior, not a hard evidence boundary. Tier 0 retrieval is implemented as a hybrid lexical + dense retrieval contract over the corpus, with application-side fusion and optional reranking behind a retrieval-profile seam, because selection scans are load-bearing for later extraction and synthesis; the information layer remains canonical, and retrieval indexes are derived, rebuildable state.

The v3.0 corpus model is deliberately collapsed. Wireframe source classes are not modelled as separate classes with lifecycle in v3.0. There is one project corpus. How a document entered is recorded as origin \- uploaded or acquired \- because origin drives provenance and egress profile. Every ingested source has an immutable source snapshot: original bytes are not retained, and frozen parsed chunks are the content of record for citation, grounding and audit. A corrected re-upload is a new snapshot, optionally marked as superseding its predecessor so consumers of the old snapshot are flagged. Library and Connected are deferred seams rather than inert v3.0 classes.

# 6\. How a run works

| Step | What happens |
| :---- | :---- |
| Start from intent | The user chooses or describes a policy intent. This may map to a template orchestration plan. |
| Plan before execution | The orchestrator proposes a human-readable plan covering capabilities, order, inputs, assumptions, dependencies, depth and steering mode. |
| Compile the executable spine | The orchestration plan compiles into the run sequence and dependency graph; downstream capability plans commit just in time when inputs exist. |
| Prepare the evidence substrate | Tier 0 work is cheap and early: snapshot, parse, segment, embed, screen, classify and appraise. Tier 1 deep extraction is scoped and capability-driven. |
| Run declared capabilities | Capability sub-agents execute their declared skeletons. Some components are deterministic or fan-out; others are agent loops over scoped tools. |
| Produce grounded blocks | Blocks expose addressable units. Claims are emitted with citations, quotes, grounding tiers and appraisal labels; gaps and patterns are also annotated. |
| Verify, steer and review | Grounding is checked; claims the cited sources do not support as worded are flagged Unsupported/mis-cited, never silently passed. Method choices log, flag or pause by steering mode; substance-shaping choices pause in every mode; remaining runtime judgements emit agent-judgement governance events. |
| Collaborate around artefacts | Collaborators inspect evidence, challenge claims and comment on anchored units. The driver steers shared state; private Q\&A remains read-only. |
| Lock, version and propagate staleness | Advancing locks an artefact version. Reruns create new versions and surface downstream blast radius through the dependency graph. |
| Read at multiple levels | Analysis is progressively disclosed: each block and artefact carries a generated, faithfulness-checked summary the user can drill from into full grounded detail. Summaries are a navigation device \- citation-free, never grounded content, and never a substitute for the detail. |
| Maintain audit and export | The decision log records plans, commits, steers, locks, reruns and supersessions. The primary surface is the tool itself; export and version-pinned deep links back into the body are a down-weighted seam, not a v3.0 build. |

Example: in a spending-proposal scrutiny project, the orchestrator might forecast Evidence Base \-\> Options Assessment \-\> Theory of Change \-\> Value for Money \-\> Risk Assessment. Evidence is ingested and appraised once, options are produced as artefact blocks, VfM consumes selected options and baseline evidence, comments attach to specific claims or rows, and a rerun surfaces which downstream artefacts are stale.

# 7\. Trust, provenance and evidence discipline

The backend treats trust as a structured state, not as inline citation theatre. Claims are typed annotations on addressable units. A claim carries its grounding tier, source references and supporting quote. Retrieval passages help find evidence, but durable citations pin to the source snapshot and verbatim supporting quote, with the located position recorded at verification \- so provenance never depends on retrieval-index internals. Evidence gaps and patterns are also annotations, because absence and corpus-shape findings can be as important as content claims in policy work.

| Trust object | Role |
| :---- | :---- |
| Grounding tier | Inference distance from evidence: direct quote; supported inference from one document; supported synthesis across sources; visibly ungrounded reasoning. Claims whose cited sources do not support them as worded are classified Unsupported/mis-cited \- a failure state, not a tier. |
| Source appraisal | Quality of the underlying source, based on document type and an extensible rubric. It is separate from the grounding tier. |
| Evidence gap | A structured assertion of absence. Its provenance records attempted search coverage rather than supporting sources. |
| Pattern | A claim about the shape of the evidence base, grounded in metadata counts or a content scan over the corpus. |
| Verification | produce-grounded-block runs synthesise \-\> cite \-\> verify \-\> write. Verification combines deterministic quote-presence checking with an LLM-as-judge grounding classifier: a tier is assigned only where the cited evidence supports the claim as worded; otherwise the claim is marked Unsupported/mis-cited. Judge I/O and prompt/model versions are persisted for eval-readiness; whether and how the judge is calibrated is owned by the eval workstream, not framed as a committed product status. |

Grounding and appraisal are not collapsed into one confidence score. A direct quote from a weak source is faithfully reported but weakly evidenced; a careful inference from strong sources has the opposite risk. The two labels imply different remedies: improve grounding by getting corroboration or regenerating from better evidence; improve appraisal by finding better sources.

The v3.0 traceability rule is deliberately honest. Every significant statement should either trace to source, be labelled as reasoning, or be labelled as a pattern grounded in a scan over the set. A statement that presents itself as source-supported but is not supported by its cited sources is Unsupported/mis-cited, whether empirical or interpretive; visibly-ungrounded reasoning is honest only because it is labelled, never a judge-certified common-knowledge safe harbour. Ungrounded or mis-cited statements masquerading as grounded evidence are the failure mode the architecture is designed to avoid.

Progressive disclosure sits alongside grounding without weakening it. Block-level and artefact-level summaries let users read at a high level and drill into detail, but a summary is a condensed rendering of the detail beneath it, not independently grounded content: it carries no citations, and its integrity property is faithfulness-to-detail, not grounding-to-source. Faithfulness is flat \- every summary is checked against the raw detail it covers, never against another summary \- and summaries sit outside the grounding economy, so they never contribute to evidence-strength roll-ups. The "what did it conclude" content a user acts on is a grounded block (the recommendation or verdict), not a summary; the summary only points at it. Faithfulness is checked by an LLM judge against the detail, with its judge I/O persisted for eval-readiness like the grounding judge; calibration is owned by the eval workstream.

# 8\. Agents, plans and human control

There is one user-facing agent surface: the persistent project orchestrator/co-pilot. It frames the task, proposes the orchestration plan, coordinates capability sub-agents, mediates check-ins, records decisions and explains what changed. Specialist capability sub-agents do the work but never speak directly to users; when they need input they park through clarify or escalate, and the orchestrator relays the request into the orchestrator thread.

Planning is two-level and progressive. The orchestration plan forecasts the whole run: capabilities, order, data flow, dependencies, overall steering and a best guess of component depth. Per-capability plans are committed just in time once inputs exist. The commit is what compiles into executable config; the forecast gives the user an understandable shape and time estimate.

| Steering mode | Meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| Minimal | Runs without proactive method stops; substance still pauses. Method flags are collated into review. |
| Moderate | Recommended default; pauses for important decisions and flags bounded method detours. |
| Frequent | Checks in at every section or block before proceeding. |

Checkpoints are steer-points, not approve/reject buttons. A user can inject reasoning, reshape outputs, challenge assumptions, override an agent verdict or ask for a rerun. Agents can choose bounded method; humans retain authority over conclusion-shaping substance. Runtime judgements not covered by declared substance gates or method hatches are routed as agent judgement calls: whether the agent continues or escalates, the routing emits a durable governance event, so continue-decisions remain reviewable after the fact.

# 9\. Collaboration, audit and versioning

Collaboration is not a replacement for Teams or Word. It is the tight evidence-anchored scrutiny loop before wider circulation. Comments are valuable because they sit next to specific claims, sections, rows, cells, gaps or sources, and because the agent can act on them: re-ground, check an alleged inaccuracy, refine or correct.

| Feature | v3.0 approach |
| :---- | :---- |
| Owner and driver | One accountable owner; one active driver for stateful commands at a time. Others watch, comment and use private Q\&A. |
| Anchored comments | Comments attach to addressable units and are structured annotations, not detached chat messages. |
| Lock-on-advance | Advancing past an artefact freezes that version. Changing it later means minting a new version \- by rerunning the capability or, once the deferred editing UX lands, by a human amendment carried as provenance/amendment state \- never editing in place. |
| Versioning | Blocks carry version chains; artefact versions are immutable snapshots of block versions; projects remain living aggregates. |
| Dependency graph | Reruns flag downstream consumers and surface blast radius rather than silently rewriting dependent artefacts. |
| Catch-me-up | A per-user projection over the Project event log since a user's last-viewed timestamp. |

The Project event log is the canonical audit spine; the decision log, per-artefact change log, version history and catch-me-up are projections over it. Governance events \- external egress per search call, agent judgement calls, material inference-route changes \- live in the same log: canonical and long-retained, excluded from the decision-log view by default. Versioned content lives in content tables, written in the same transaction as its corresponding event, and is referenced by log events. Transcripts are persisted as companion records for continuity and nuance, but they are not the source of truth. Load-bearing chat is promoted into structured state at capture time.

# 10\. Execution, observability, security and v3.0 build posture

The v3.0 execution substrate is intentionally build-light. Runs move off the request path into an off-request worker tier. LangGraph provides the fixed reasoning harness and durable checkpoints on Postgres. A runs table holds status and pending human signals. Tool results are memoised. Checkpoints sit at block or component boundaries. The canonical Project event log remains separate from LangGraph execution checkpoints.

Serial v3.0 does not mean no parallelism anywhere. Orchestration branches are serial, but data-parallel fan-out inside evidence tools \- appraising or extracting over many documents \- is retained. Branch-level parallelism is deferred until the product needs it.

| Area | Commitment |
| :---- | :---- |
| Canonical audit plane | Project event log (including governance events) and structured state: long-retained, FOI-facing, source of truth for what happened and why; the decision log is its audit-facing projection. |
| Operational telemetry plane | LLM traces, application metrics, worker health, cost, latency and errors: non-canonical, sensitivity-bound, shorter-retained. |
| Langfuse trace backbone | Carried forward from v2; maps naturally to tool \-\> component \-\> capability \-\> artefact \-\> project. |
| Eval readiness | Observable I/O at boundaries, declared contracts, eval results attached to addressable units, and human signals (including citation validations and challenges) captured as feedback and sampling inputs \- not calibration labels; judge calibration is owned by the eval workstream. |
| v3.0 operations | Health checks, basic alerting, an eval-capable CI harness (suites become merge-blocking once adopted by the eval workstream; deterministic engineering tests run in normal CI), retention and PII masking for telemetry, and access control on observability tooling. |

Security is handled primarily at deployment, configured-tool and inference-route level in v3.0. v3.0 has live egress: inference calls through the configured inference route (first pass: the OpenAI API under approved data controls; target: Amazon Bedrock as model availability and region allow), and search queries to configured external evidence backends. Search-query egress is logged as a canonical governance event so project owners can inspect what left the system where appropriate; high-volume inference calls remain in operational telemetry, while the active inference route and its data-control posture are recorded canonically. The posture is own-AWS hosting, database in the same AWS environment, open-source code and an in-house inference routing layer over configured routes as the key future-proofing seam. Per-item sensitivity gates remain deferred until sensitivity labels drive concrete behaviour such as blocking, approval, query generalisation, route selection or private deployment \- deferring them avoids an inert security label that implies protection the system does not yet enforce.

# 11\. What this means for the team

| Implementation rule | Why it matters |
| :---- | :---- |
| Build around artefacts and blocks | Do not treat outputs as flat markdown. Artefacts, blocks and addressable units are the foundation for provenance, comments, versions, future export/share seams and evals. |
| Treat the plan as canonical | Do not create a hidden execution truth. Machine config must compile from approved plan fields and record material divergences. |
| Keep provenance structured | Claims, citations, supporting quotes, gaps, patterns, comments and evals should be queryable annotations, not inline text conventions. |
| Scope agent tools aggressively | Agents should see only the tools declared for their current component plus the tiny universal core. |
| Preserve method/substance routing | Substance-shaping choices pause in every mode. Method deviations log, flag or pause based on declared hatches and steering mode. |
| Avoid inert model distinctions | No strand entity, no v3.0 source-class lifecycle, no per-item sensitivity flag without behaviour, no status badge for processes outside the tool. |
| Separate audit from telemetry | The Project event log is canonical (the decision log is its audit-facing projection). Traces and metrics are operational. Eval results bridge the two by attaching to canonical units. |
| Build light but seamful | Use the v3.0 worker/checkpointer model, but keep durable execution and inference behind interfaces for later swap-out. |

The architectural north star: make the system fast enough to be used in live policy work, structured enough to inspect under scrutiny, and bounded enough that human judgement remains accountable.

# Appendix A. v3.0 commitments and deferred seams

| Area | v3.0 | Deferred seam |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Project output | Decision-support body with cited artefacts, live provenance and progressively-disclosed block/artefact summaries. | External white-paper policing, cross-boundary traceability, and export/sharing with version-pinned deep links. |
| Data model | Projects, artefacts, blocks, addressable units, annotations, tags/scoping, origin; block/artefact summaries as faithfulness-checked renderings outside the grounding economy. | Statement-to-statement cross-artefact tracing, chart view-types, richer source libraries, summaries as retrieval-routing signal. |
| Evidence | Tier 0 substrate early; Tier 1 extraction scoped and capability-driven. | Broad mandatory deep extraction and full deterministic scoring for every capability. |
| Agents | One orchestrator, declared capability sub-agents, scoped tools, universal core. | General-purpose autonomous agent platform or global tool palette. |
| Execution | Serial orchestration, worker tier, LangGraph checkpoints, runs table, memoisation. | Dedicated durable workflow engine, branch-level parallelism, durable timers. |
| Collaboration | Owner, driver, collaborators, anchored comments, private Q\&A, lock-on-advance. | Formal sign-off, clearance workflow, artefact-scoped permissions, cross-project nudges. |
| Observability | Langfuse trace spine, basic APM, eval-capable CI harness, SLI alerts, PII/retention policy. | Formal SLO/SLA, incident process, canaries, live drift monitors, product analytics. |
| Security | Own-AWS, configured inference routes behind an in-house routing layer, deployment-level sensitivity with logged search-query egress. | Private deployments, self-host model path, per-item egress controls. |

# Appendix B. Shared glossary

| Term | Meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| Project | The top-level policy workstream; not a single search or report. |
| Decision-support body | The project output: artefacts, corpus, provenance, comments, versions, dependencies and decision log. |
| Corpus | The source documents and evidence/data held in the information layer for the project. |
| Information layer | Shared substrate containing the corpus (as source snapshots with frozen parsed chunks as the content of record), artefacts, metadata, embeddings, appraisals, the queryable extracted-findings layer and retrieval/scoping state. |
| Capability | An artefact-producing composition of components, tools, dependencies and output shape. |
| Component | A step inside a capability skeleton, owned and run by that capability's expert sub-agent. |
| Tool | A shared callable operation with declared input/output; exposed only when declared for a component. |
| Artefact | The visible unit of value produced by a capability. |
| Block | The unit of storage, versioning, interaction, commenting and regeneration. |
| Addressable unit | A span, row, cell or stable sub-block unit that annotations can attach to. |
| Annotation | Structured record attached to a unit: claim, citation, gap, pattern, comment or eval score. |
| Summary | A generated, faithfulness-checked condensed rendering of a block or artefact for progressive disclosure; citation-free, outside the grounding economy, never a substitute for the grounded detail it points at. |
| Grounding tier | Inference distance between a statement and evidence; Unsupported/mis-cited is the separate failure state for claims their cited sources do not support. |
| Appraisal | Source-quality assessment, separate from grounding tier. |
| Orchestrator | The single user-facing co-pilot that owns the conversation and orchestration plan. |
| Project event log | The single canonical append-only spine for project lifecycle, decision and governance events; the decision log, change log, version history and catch-me-up are projections over it. |
| Decision log | Audit-facing projection of the Project event log: plans, steers, commits, locks, reruns and supersessions. |
